name: THE LIVERY STABLE
materialIdentity: Weathered plank, straw and leather under one lantern, night (errata 88 A)

entrances.note: In by the stable doors, at left: Lower Street leads here.

LOOK_AT.say: The chair, tipped back at the angle of a man who's seen everything once. Now he's seen me twice.
A kitchen chair tipped back against the wall at the exact angle of a man who has seen everything once.
repeat: The back legs are worn short. He has tipped it for so many years the chair has adapted.
It faces Grievance's stall. He sits where he can see her. I've yet to see her return the courtesy.

LISTEN_TO.say: A creak as it settles back onto four legs.
repeat: Nothing. It's waiting for him, and it can wait.
The chair ticks against the wall in the draft, as if he were still in it, rocking.

LOOK_AT.say: Who has hired what, going back years. Twelve years ago somebody hired Grievance for four days and did not write down where they were going.
repeat: Names, dates and animals, in a hand that gets more patient every year.
Some names have a line through them and the word PAID. Some have a line and the word GONE.
Nothing. Paper pinned to wood, keeping accounts.
The pin rattles in the draft. Twelve years of comings and goings, held up by one nail.

LOOK_AT.say: Her blanket, striped, older than the stable. It is hers the way the territory is the government's: nominally, and at her pleasure.
repeat: A blanket, folded, considerably better than the blanket on my bed.
It smells of mule, and of something older, like a coat kept in a cedar chest.

LISTEN_TO.say: Wool and straw. A warm quiet.
repeat: Nothing.
Nothing. It is the quietest thing in the stable, and it knows its worth.

overrides.PICK_UP: She turned her head one inch. I returned the blanket two inches. We understand each other.

LOOK_AT.say: Oats, at a level she monitors precisely. The livery man says she can count.
repeat: The lid has a latch she has learned to work and a second latch she has decided not to, as a courtesy.
The level hasn't gone down while I've been here. She's watching me watch it.

LISTEN_TO.say: A shift of grain. She heard me look.
repeat: Grain settling, then a snort from the stall to let me know it was noted.
Nothing. She has stopped listening for me, which I take as a promotion.

LOOK_AT.say: A shoeing anvil, cold more days than not.
repeat: The face is worn into a shallow dish by forty years of hammering. It has outlasted every horse it shod.
A horseshoe hangs on the horn, half made. The smith left in the middle of a sentence.
then: The ring of it, they say, used to be the town's clock.

LISTEN_TO.say: Nothing. It is saving its one note.
repeat: Nothing, though I can hear it anyway: a high clean A, if it's any good. I'm not going to strike it to find out. I want to.
Nothing. An anvil at rest is the quietest iron there is.

overrides.PICK_UP: It occurred to me. It stopped occurring to me almost immediately.

LOOK_AT.say: Her name is burned into the post. The other stalls are numbered.
repeat: Her stall is swept and the others are not. The livery man has priorities, and they are a mule.
There are tooth marks along the top board. She has been working on it for years, without hurry.
then: Somebody, at some point, decided this animal warranted a name.

repeat: Her tail swishing, at a tempo she sets.
Nothing. She is standing very still, which is how she listens.
Her ears follow me round the stable. The rest of her does not consider me worth turning for.
She is the color of a wet saddle, and she is wearing her own opinion of me.
then: She has looked at me once, fully, and reached a verdict she sees no reason to revisit.

LISTEN_TO.say: Breathing, slow and deliberate. She is not asleep.
repeat: Nothing. She is holding her breath. I am almost certain she is holding her breath.
A long breath out through the nose. It is the most eloquent opinion anyone in this town has given me.

overrides.USE: I don't use Grievance. I am, if she consents, briefly adjacent to her purposes.
overrides.PUSH: I've pushed buildings with more give.

LOOK_AT.say: Four mules, numbered, entirely willing to work. They are looking at Grievance the way a work crew looks at a man who has got away with something.
repeat: Number Three is asleep standing up. Number One is pretending to be.
They are good mules. Nobody will ever name them.
Chewing, in four slightly different rhythms.
One of them sighs. It is a working sigh, and it means nothing by it.

LOOK_AT.say: Harness, bridles, and collars, hung by size.
repeat: Harness, in good repair, hung in order. Whoever runs this stable is better at their trade than anybody else in town is at theirs.
One collar is enormous. It belonged to a horse the livery man still talks about, and nobody has oiled it since.
then: A history of horses this town no longer has.

LISTEN_TO.say: Leather straps, touching in the draft. A dry conversation.
repeat: Leather. Nothing.
A buckle tapping in the draft, keeping a slow time of its own.

LOOK_AT.say: Hay above, gold below, if you ask the loft ladder, which is worn brighter than any pew in the church.
repeat: Men sleep up there, by the look of the ladder, and the livery man does not ask.
Hay, and dust in the light, and the smell of a summer that happened somewhere else.

LISTEN_TO.say: Straw settling, and something small making a home in it.
repeat: A rustle, a squeak, and a silence that is pretending to be hay.
Nothing up there now. Whoever sleeps in it is out working, or trying to.

overrides.USE: The ladder is worn bright by men sleeping off their optimism. I've got a room. For now. I insist on the distinction.

LOOK_AT.say: Six stalls, one occupied, and the town's whole history in the others. I know which parts of it were true now. Not many.
Six stalls, one occupied. The others hold hay, a broken sulky, and the general storage of a town that keeps everything.
repeat: The broken sulky has a seat for one and a wheel for nobody.
One stall is stacked with folding chairs, which the town keeps here against the next funeral.

LISTEN_TO.say: Boards, warm and creaking. The building digests.
repeat: A mouse in the empty stalls, taking inventory.
The boards again, warm and slow. The stable sounds like a big animal at rest.

exits.name: THE STABLE DOORS

LOOK_AT.say: Doors wide enough for a coach, opened to a gap wide enough for a man. The territory in one hinge.
repeat: The hinges are new and the doors are not. Somebody repairs what moves and leaves what doesn't.
Grievance can see out through the gap from her stall. I suspect that is why it is that wide and no wider.

LISTEN_TO.say: Wind through the gap, asking to come in. The doors hold their line.
repeat: Main Street, narrowed to the width of the gap.
The wind, still asking. The doors, still saying no.

exits.note: Errata 161 (errata 43's three streets): the livery opens off Lower Street.

PICK_UP.say: He has lifted every animal in this stable at one time or another. I am not going to give him the satisfaction of the comparison.

PUSH.say: He is tipped back on two chair legs. One push and we would both learn something.

USE.say: You do not use the livery man. You apply, like everybody else.

lamps.note: The lantern on the post by Grievance's stall. A slow, low breath (invariant 9).
